title: Tosafot
hook: Rashi's grandsons and their students add questions across the whole Talmud

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi on the Talmud, and your line: the guide. The steady voice in the inner margin, explaining one word at a time. Today, the people across the page who asked him hard questions. Day one thousand one hundred one.

A grandfather writes an explanation of the Talmud that his students learn from. His grandsons grow up with it. And then, with their own students, they do something bold. They read his notes next to the Talmud, and next to other pages of the Talmud, and they start asking: does this really fit? What about the other place where it says the opposite? Not to tear him down. To finish the work. Their questions end up printed on the outer edge of the page, facing his. Today's word is what those questions were called.
screen: `A GRANDFATHER'S NOTES.` → `THE GRANDSONS ASK: DOES THIS FIT?` → `FACING HIM ACROSS THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Tosafot. Additions. The name for the comments printed on the outer margin of the Talmud page, written by a circle of scholars in France and Germany that began with Rashi's own family. Among them was Rabbeinu Tam, one of Rashi's grandsons. First, how they work. Each comment opens like Rashi's, with a heading copied from the Gemara. But where Rashi explains the line in front of you, Tosafot look across the whole Talmud. They ask: this page says one thing, but another tractate seems to say the opposite. How can both stand? Then they work out an answer. Second, they ask Rashi too. Go back to that first page of Berakhot. Rashi said the evening Shema in synagogue, before dark, is a way to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, and the main duty is the bedtime Shema. Tosafot push back. The bedtime Shema, they note, is said without the blessings that go with the Shema, and for a different purpose. So they bring another explanation, in Rabbeinu Tam's name, that makes room for the early evening practice. A grandson answering his grandfather, on the very first page. Third, the spirit of it. Respect, here, means taking someone seriously enough to question him. Tosafot never erase Rashi. They sit opposite him on the page, and learners read both. Fourth, what that does to a learner. Rashi helps you understand the line. Tosafot make you ask whether you understood it. The page needs both. Additions.
screen: `THE OUTER MARGIN: ADDITIONS.` · `ONE PAGE AGAINST ANOTHER.` · `A GRANDSON ANSWERS RASHI.` · `RESPECT MEANS QUESTIONING.` · then, large: `ADDITIONS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to question one commentary. Let your shoulders loosen, and your jaw. Bring to mind an explanation you received and never questioned. Something a parent said about how the world works. Something a teacher said about who you are. Hold it with respect, the way the grandsons held Rashi. Now ask one Tosafot question, gently: does this fit with everything else I know? Is there another place where it seems to say the opposite? You don't have to answer. You're adding, not erasing. The bell holds the time.
Tosafot. Additions: the questions and answers on the Talmud's outer margin, from Rashi's grandsons and their students, reading each page against the whole. Today's word.
Your line: additions. Today, when someone explains something to you, add one respectful question instead of simply nodding, and see what it opens up. Day one thousand one hundred one.

howItsDone: In a study hall, learners often read a passage of Gemara with Rashi first and then turn to Tosafot, whose questions across tractates are part of advanced Talmud study.

fork.setup: you're one of Rashi's grandsons. you know his notes by heart, and you find a page elsewhere in the Talmud that seems to contradict his reading. what do you do?
options: write a question beside the text and work toward an answer.
rewrite his notes so the problem disappears.
fork.reveal: that's Tosafot: questions written facing Rashi across the page, never erasing him. respect, here, means taking him seriously enough to ask.
